summary.text: A polynomial ring is a ring formed from polynomials in one or more indeterminates, with coefficients in another ring, often a field.
Its importance rests on the many properties it shares with the ring of the integers.
Polynomial rings occur, and are often fundamental, in number theory, commutative algebra and algebraic geometry.

facts.label: The indeterminate
facts.value: X has no value other than itself and cannot vary

facts.label: Degree
facts.value: The largest k for which the coefficient of Xᵏ is nonzero

facts.label: Division
facts.value: A unique pair (q, r) gives a = bq + r

facts.label: Units
facts.value: Over an integral domain, units are the constants that are units in the base ring

items.prompt: You divide one polynomial by another with long division and keep going until the leftover piece is small enough. What counts as small enough?

options.label: It is zero or has lower degree than the divisor
It has the same degree as the divisor
It is a constant, whatever the divisor is
It has a leading coefficient of 1

items.explain: Dividing a by b ≠ 0 gives a unique pair (q, r) with a = bq + r, where either r = 0 or deg(r) < deg(b): the remainder is zero or has smaller degree than the divisor.

items.prompt: A student writes X equals 3 inside the definition of the polynomial ring and then computes. Why is this not how X behaves in the ring?

options.label: X can only be replaced by 0 or 1
X must take every value at the same time
X is a constant that varies with the coefficients
X has no value other than itself and cannot vary

items.explain: In the polynomial ring, X is an indeterminate: a symbol with no value other than itself, so it is a constant of the ring rather than a variable.

items.prompt: Over a field with only finitely many elements, can two different polynomials give exactly the same function on that field?

options.label: No, different polynomials always give different functions
Yes, but only the zero polynomial can do it
Yes, this can happen, unlike over an infinite field
No, but only because the field is finite

items.explain: Over an infinite field different polynomials define different functions, but this is false for finite fields; for instance, if K has q elements, the polynomials 0 and X^q − X both give the zero function.

items.prompt: The coefficients come from an integral domain. Which polynomials have a multiplicative inverse in the polynomial ring?

options.label: Every polynomial with leading coefficient 1
Every polynomial of degree one
Constant polynomials that are units in the coefficient ring
Every polynomial with a nonzero constant term

items.explain: Over an integral domain, a polynomial is a unit if and only if it is constant and is a unit in the coefficient ring.

items.prompt: A polynomial can be written as a product of two non-constant polynomials. How should it be described?

options.label: Irreducible
Not irreducible
Monic
Constant

items.explain: A polynomial is irreducible if it is not the product of two non-constant polynomials, so one that is such a product is not irreducible.

items.prompt: When the coefficients form a field, what mainly explains why the polynomial ring behaves so much like the integers?

options.label: Long division works for polynomials much as for integers
Both rings contain only finitely many elements
Both rings let you divide by any nonzero element
Both rings are made only of constant terms

items.explain: Most of the similarities with the integers come from the similarity between long division of integers and long division of polynomials.

paragraphs.heading: What a polynomial ring is
paragraphs.text: A polynomial ring is a ring built out of polynomials. The polynomials can use one or more indeterminates, the letters that are traditionally also called variables. Their coefficients come from some other ring, and that ring is often a field. When people say "polynomial ring" with no more detail, they often mean the special case with a single indeterminate over a field.

paragraphs.heading: What its elements look like
paragraphs.text: The ring with indeterminate X and coefficients in K is written K[X]. One way to describe it is as the set of all expressions p = p₀ + p₁X + p₂X² + ⋯ + pₘXᵐ, where m is a nonnegative integer and every coefficient belongs to K. The powers of X follow the familiar exponent rules, such as X⁰ = 1 and Xᵏ⋅Xˡ = Xᵏ⁺ˡ. Here X has no value apart from itself and does not vary; inside the ring it is a constant. Two polynomials are equal when their coefficients for each power of X match.

paragraphs.heading: Adding and multiplying
paragraphs.text: You can also picture K[X] as K with one new element X brought in from outside. That X commutes with every element of K and has no other special properties. Polynomials are added and multiplied by the ordinary rules of algebra: the sum adds matching coefficients, rᵢ = pᵢ + qᵢ, and the product has coefficients sᵢ = p₀qᵢ + p₁qᵢ₋₁ + ⋯ + pᵢq₀. Together with multiplying by a scalar, these operations meet all the axioms that a commutative algebra over K must satisfy. That is why polynomial rings are also called polynomial algebras.

paragraphs.heading: Degree and special polynomials
paragraphs.text: The degree of a polynomial p, written deg(p), is the largest k for which the coefficient of Xᵏ is not zero. The zero polynomial, whose coefficients are all zero, is handled in different ways: its degree has been left undefined, set to −1, or set to −∞. A constant polynomial is either the zero polynomial or one of degree zero. A nonzero polynomial is called monic when its leading coefficient is 1. When K is an integral domain, a polynomial has a multiplicative inverse only if it is a constant that already has one in K.

paragraphs.heading: A close cousin of the integers
paragraphs.text: When K is a field, K[X] shares many properties with the ring of integers ℤ. Most of these likenesses come from long division, which works for polynomials much as it does for whole numbers. Given polynomials a and b with b ≠ 0, there is exactly one pair (q, r) with a = bq + r, where r is either zero or of smaller degree than b. This makes K[X] a Euclidean domain. Most other Euclidean domains, apart from the integers, have neither this uniqueness nor an easy method like long division. Most of these properties stop holding if K is not a field, or if there are several indeterminates.

paragraphs.heading: Where they show up
paragraphs.text: Polynomial rings turn up across mathematics and are often basic to areas such as number theory, commutative algebra and algebraic geometry. Many kinds of rings in ring theory, such as unique factorization domains and graded rings, were introduced to generalize some properties of polynomial rings. One subtle point is that a polynomial is not the same thing as the function it defines. Over an infinite field, different polynomials give different functions. Over a field with q elements, though, the polynomials 0 and X^q − X both give the zero function.
